name: Rosa Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27, have a bachelor’s degree and lead five liability-claims clerks at an insurer. I earn above the usual rate because I catch contradictions in witness accounts before decisions go out, and I have never used AI tools. I rent a flat alone, have no children and have saved eleven months of expenses. There are plenty of insurers nearby; outside work I attend church and like a dependable routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the liability-claims team that a filing shortcut is fine, but a witness statement still needs a patient reader. I have never used AI tools and would keep the signed account beside every claim decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I supervise five clerks and earn above the usual rate because I catch dates that do not match across witness accounts. I rent alone, have no children and have saved eleven months of expenses, so I can pay my own bills while this job stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my Wednesday check of ten disputed incident reports and save 200 a month while the present wage holds. In the first year I would compare any machine-filed statements with the signed accounts before approving a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own work and rent. A witness can remember the right event and still write down the wrong Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which date dispute stayed with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shop owner said a delivery fell on Monday, but the carrier log showed Tuesday. I called both parties before the claim letter went out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a junior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the junior clerk to put the two dates side by side. The point is to ask one more question before denying a bill.

say: I would keep **signed witness accounts** beside claim decisions.
I would continue **Wednesday incident checks** before letters go out.
think: I have **eleven months saved** and above-typical pay.
I still need **my present wage** to keep that reserve intact.
do: **Check ten disputed reports** each Wednesday against signed witness accounts.
**Save 200 monthly** while my current wage covers rent.
feel: **Calm** about present paid work and rent.
S0.quote: A witness can remember the right event and still write down the wrong Tuesday.
fieldNote: Her **date-checking skill** catches conflicting witness accounts and calls parties before liability letters are sent.
Her **eleven-month reserve** supports current rent and food security while her higher paid job continues.

steps.text: Check ten disputed liability reports each Wednesday against signed accounts
Save 200 monthly while current wage continues covering rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say Steady Disruption could let AI write liability letters and compare statements before our team opens a file. Employers should keep a named person responsible for a wrong denial. The claimants cannot argue with a queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own lead hours could be cut if one clerk checks several automatic files. Eleven months saved gives me time, and there are many insurers nearby, but none has offered me another paid role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my manager next week for written paid review hours and a named appeal contact. I would keep the incident log myself; if my hours are cut, I would check posted local liability jobs for real hours and enough net pay for rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own hours but not trapped. I have worked for the pay in that reserve, and I do not want a new target to spend it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether a denial is checked against the signed account before it goes to a customer. A written name and paid hours matter more to me than a training slogan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try another insurer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not take an unpaid trial at another insurer. I need a posted wage and enough hours to cover the flat.

say: I would demand **named appeal responsibility** and paid review hours.
I would keep **signed statements** available for human checks.
think: I could lose **lead hours** despite strong past savings.
I cannot assume **nearby insurers** have actual paid vacancies.
do: **Ask manager next week** for written paid review hours and appeal contact.
**Keep incident log** while current role pays.
**Check posted local jobs** if hours fall and net pay covers essentials.
S1.quote: The claimants cannot argue with a queue.
fieldNote: Her **manager request** is for written responsibilities and paid review time, not a granted promise.
Her **local search** begins after hours fall and requires an actual bill-covering post.

steps.text: Keep disputed incident log while current role pays
Check posted local liability roles if hours fall and net pay covers rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2028 could read witness accounts, price liability claims and write decisions cheaper than our team. Robots doing site inspection might follow around 2031, but our office work faces the earlier year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead post could disappear, although I have no cut notice yet. Eleven months saved is time to look for paid work; I will not call it a wage or count on relatives to pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for written staffing notice now and keep the reserve for rent. If the job ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply only to posted paid local customer-service or claims roles where I meet the requirements and net pay covers bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible loss of my own wage, but I have a plan and time to search. An address book full of insurers is not a payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sort of other role would count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would accept a customer-service role only if it has a real contract, paid hours and enough net income. AGI could take its desk tasks too, so I would read the job duties carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your community help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could ask my church friends about actual openings, not for a promise to support me. I would keep rent decisions on my own wages and savings.

say: I would warn that **office claims work** faces AGI by 2028.
I would place **site robots later**, around 2031.
think: My **lead post could go** without any cut notice yet.
I cannot treat **eleven months saved** as a new wage.
do: **Request written staffing notice** and keep reserve for rent now.
**Apply after 2028 loss** only to qualified paid local roles with bill-covering net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible wage loss, with a funded search window.
S2.quote: An address book full of insurers is not a payslip.
fieldNote: Her **job loss remains possible**, not certain, and she has eleven months of expenses saved.
She may ask **church friends for leads**, without assuming money, a vacancy or a lasting desk role.

steps.text: Request written staffing notice and hold eleven-month reserve for rent
Apply to qualified paid local roles after 2028 loss if net pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to train people for work that still needs judgement and to put appeal duties in writing. Robots inspecting incident sites might follow around 2034, after the desk changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would consider a traditional claims apprenticeship for younger staff, but I have a bachelor’s degree and a lead wage to protect. A short unpaid placement would be a pay cut, not a career plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a local repair assessor for a real paid trainee vacancy and its safety requirements, and ask my employer whether it would protect my hours for supervised visits. If both agree in writing I would train; after 2031 job loss I would apply only if qualified and take-home pay after travel covers rent, food and basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about eventual wage risk, but five years lets me check the trade properly. A trainee badge does not cover my rent by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the training real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to know who pays the supervisor, what safety training is required and how many hours are guaranteed. If those are missing I would keep the claims job and save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would site work last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Around 2034, robots could inspect incident sites too. I would treat the assessor route as paid work while it exists, not a forever answer.

say: I would seek **paid supervised assessment** at an actual firm with written safety rules.
I would protect **current lead hours** before any supervised field training begins.
think: I need **an actual trainee vacancy**, not an unpaid badge.
I know **site robots** may follow around 2034.
do: **Check paid trainee vacancy** and written safety requirements now.
**Request protected paid visits** and train only if both employers agree.
**Apply after 2031 loss** only if qualified take-home pay after travel covers rent, food and basic bills.
feel: **Anxious** about later pay, with time to test a route.
S3.quote: A trainee badge does not cover my rent by itself.
fieldNote: Her **training requires** a posted paid trainee role and written protection of present hours.
The **assessor bridge** still faces physical robots about three years after AGI.

steps.text: Check actual paid assessor trainee vacancy and written safety requirements
Train on supervised visits only if both employers protect paid hours
Apply after 2031 loss if qualified pay after travel covers rent food and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to save, train apprentices and make appeal duties clear. Robots at incident sites may follow around 2039; office work changes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My rent and wage feel secure for the next few years, though I am only 27 and need decades of earnings. I would rather build a bigger reserve than gamble on one supposedly safe job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep Wednesday incident checks and save 250 monthly while the high wage continues. I would ask the manager annually for paid appeal staffing figures; after 2036 job loss, I would check actual qualified local openings with net pay above my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about later work but safe over the next few years. Ten years lets me fill the savings jar without pretending it is a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which annual figure matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how many people are paid to review disputed denials. A list of training plans without paid places is not a staffing plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move or borrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep renting until a real offer and a written budget justify a move. I will not borrow for a course that has no posted job at the end.

say: I would ask for **paid appeal staffing** before AGI in 2036.
I would keep **signed incident checks** in the workflow.
think: I feel **secure near term** on high current pay.
I still need **future wages** beyond this claims title.
do: **Check incident reports** each Wednesday while current job pays.
Ask annually for **paid staffing** and check qualified local openings after loss.
feel: **Uneasy** later, secure over the next few years.
S4.quote: A list of training plans without paid places is not a staffing plan.
fieldNote: Her **long runway** supports saving from present pay, without implying a pension.
Later **job applications** require qualified actual openings and enough net pay for bills.

steps.text: Check ten disputed incident reports every Wednesday while role pays
Save 250 monthly while current high salary continues
Ask manager annually for paid appeal staffing figures
Check qualified posted local jobs after 2036 loss if net pay covers bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead post could disappear before a paid assessor route is proven. Written notice, a qualified local contract covering rent and a paid supervised training place would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who is responsible when a wrong denial leaves our desk. I want a real name on the letter, not a queue number.

headlineQuote: I want a real name on the letter, not a queue number.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old liability lead** with a bachelor’s degree, high pay and eleven months saved.
She rents **alone**, attends church and has never used AI tools.
She prizes **signed witness accounts** and a named person responsible for denials.
She considers **paid supervised assessment** only with safety requirements, protected hours and a real vacancy.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her lead post before a paid assessor route is proven.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a rent-covering contract and paid supervised training would help.
